name: Eczema (atopic eczema)
overview: Atopic eczema is a common long-term condition that makes the skin itchy, dry and cracked. It often starts in childhood and may improve with age. There is no cure, but treatments and good skin care can control it.
symptoms: Itchy, dry, cracked or sore skin
Patches that may look red on lighter skin or darker brown, purple or grey on darker skin
Commonly on the hands, inside the elbows, behind the knees, and on the face and scalp in children
Flare-ups when symptoms get worse
causes: A mix of genes and a skin barrier that loses moisture easily
Flare-ups triggered by soaps, detergents, stress, weather changes, infections or allergens
riskFactors: Family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses eczema by looking at the skin and asking about symptoms and family history.
treatment: Emollients (moisturisers) used every day
Topical steroid creams for flare-ups
Other creams or tablets prescribed by a doctor or dermatologist for severe eczema
Antibiotics if the skin becomes infected
selfCare: Use emollients often, including instead of soap
Avoid triggers such as perfumed products
Keep nails short and avoid scratching
prevention: Regular emollient use to reduce flare-ups
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you or your child has eczema
Eczema is not improving with treatment
Skin looks infected: weeping, crusting or painful
emergencySigns: Painful eczema that is getting worse quickly, with fluid-filled blisters and feeling unwell or feverish (possible eczema herpeticum)

name: Psoriasis
overview: Psoriasis is a long-term skin condition that causes flaky patches of skin covered in scales. It is linked to the immune system and tends to come and go in flare-ups. It is not contagious, and many treatments are available.
symptoms: Raised, flaky patches of skin with silvery-white scales
Patches may look pink or red on lighter skin and purple or dark brown on darker skin
Commonly on elbows, knees, scalp and lower back
Itching or soreness
Pitted or discoloured nails
Joint pain and swelling in some people (psoriatic arthritis)
causes: An immune system problem that speeds up skin cell production
Genes play a part
Flare-ups triggered by stress, injury to the skin, infections, alcohol, smoking or some medicines
diagnosis: A GP usually diagnoses psoriasis by looking at the skin, scalp and nails.
treatment: Creams and ointments, including emollients, steroid creams and vitamin D-based creams
Light therapy (phototherapy)
Tablets or injections that act on the immune system for more severe psoriasis
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you have psoriasis
Treatment is not working
Painful, swollen or stiff joints
emergencySigns: Widespread red, inflamed skin over most of the body with feeling very unwell or a high temperature
Widespread pus-filled spots with fever

name: Acne
overview: Acne is a common skin condition that causes spots, oily skin and sometimes skin that is hot or painful to touch. It most often affects teenagers but can continue into adulthood. Effective treatments are available.
symptoms: Blackheads and whiteheads
Red or darker spots (papules) and pus-filled spots
Large, painful lumps under the skin (nodules or cysts)
Mostly on the face, back and chest
Oily skin and possible scarring
causes: Hair follicles becoming blocked by oil and dead skin cells
Hormonal changes, especially during puberty
Bacteria in blocked follicles causing inflammation
riskFactors: Hormonal changes such as periods, pregnancy or PCOS
diagnosis: A GP or pharmacist diagnoses acne by looking at the skin.
treatment: Pharmacy creams and gels for mild acne
Prescription creams, antibiotic tablets or hormonal contraceptives
Specialist treatment for severe acne, prescribed by a dermatologist
selfCare: Wash the affected area gently twice a day
Do not squeeze or pick spots
Be patient: treatments can take weeks to work
prevention: Start treatment early to reduce scarring
whenToSeeDoctor: Pharmacy treatments have not worked
Acne is moderate or severe, painful, or causing scarring
Acne is affecting your mood or confidence

name: Rosacea
overview: Rosacea is a common long-term skin condition that mainly affects the face, causing redness, flushing and sometimes spots. Symptoms often come and go. Treatment and avoiding triggers can help control it.
symptoms: Redness across the cheeks, nose, chin and forehead (may be harder to see on darker skin)
Flushing that comes and goes
Visible small blood vessels
Spots and bumps
Burning or stinging skin
Dry, irritated or gritty eyes
causes: The exact cause is unknown
Triggers include sunlight, hot or cold weather, alcohol, spicy food, hot drinks, stress and exercise
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses rosacea by looking at the skin and asking about symptoms and triggers.
treatment: Creams and gels prescribed by a doctor
Antibiotic tablets for spots
Laser or light treatment for visible blood vessels
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent facial redness or flushing
Spots or skin thickening on the nose
Eye symptoms such as dryness or irritation
emergencySigns: Painful red eye with changes in vision

name: Athlete's foot
overview: Athlete's foot is a common fungal infection that affects the feet, especially between the toes. It is usually not serious and can be treated with pharmacy antifungal creams, sprays or powders.
symptoms: Itchy white patches between the toes
Red, sore and flaky patches on the feet (may be less visible on darker skin)
Cracked, bleeding skin
Fluid-filled blisters in some cases
causes: Fungal infection that thrives in warm, damp places
Spread by walking barefoot in places like changing rooms or sharing towels
riskFactors: Diabetes or a weakened immune system
diagnosis: A pharmacist or GP diagnoses athlete's foot by looking at the skin; a skin sample is rarely needed.
treatment: Antifungal creams, sprays or powders from a pharmacy
Prescription treatment if pharmacy products do not work
selfCare: Dry feet carefully, especially between the toes
Use a separate towel for your feet
Wear clean cotton socks and change them daily
Keep using treatment for the recommended time after symptoms clear
prevention: Wear flip-flops in communal showers and changing rooms
Do not share towels, socks or shoes
whenToSeeDoctor: Pharmacy treatment has not worked after 2 weeks
You have diabetes or a weakened immune system
Foot is red, hot and swollen (possible cellulitis)

name: Fungal nail infection
overview: Fungal nail infections are common, especially in toenails. They are not usually serious but can take a long time to treat.
symptoms: Discoloured nail, often white, black, yellow or green
Thickened or misshapen nail
Brittle nail that crumbles
Nail lifting from the nail bed
Pain or discomfort in some cases
causes: Fungal infection, often spreading from athlete's foot
Fungi that thrive in warm, moist places
diagnosis: A doctor may diagnose it by looking at the nail and sending a nail clipping for testing.
treatment: Antifungal nail paint from a pharmacy for mild infections
Antifungal tablets prescribed by a doctor
Laser treatment or nail removal in some cases
selfCare: Keep nails short and feet clean and dry
prevention: Do not share nail clippers or towels
whenToSeeDoctor: Treatment from a pharmacy has not worked
The infection is spreading or painful
You have diabetes or a weakened immune system

name: Scabies
overview: Scabies is a common skin condition caused by tiny mites that burrow into the skin. It causes intense itching, especially at night. It spreads easily through close skin contact and is treated with creams or lotions applied to the whole body.
symptoms: Intense itching, especially at night
A raised rash or spots
Tiny lines (burrows) on the skin, often between the fingers
Rash commonly on the hands, wrists, armpits, waist and genitals
causes: Infestation with Sarcoptes scabiei mites
Spread by prolonged skin-to-skin contact or, less often, shared bedding and clothing
riskFactors: Close contact with an infected person
diagnosis: A pharmacist or GP diagnoses scabies by looking at the rash and burrows.
treatment: Insecticide cream or lotion applied to the whole body, then repeated after a week
Everyone in the household should be treated at the same time
Tablets prescribed by a doctor in some cases
selfCare: Wash bedding, towels and clothes on a hot wash on the day of the first treatment
Seal items that cannot be washed in a bag for 3 days
Avoid close contact until 24 hours after the first treatment
prevention: Treat all close contacts at the same time
Avoid sharing bedding, towels or clothes with someone who has scabies
whenToSeeDoctor: Itching continues more than 4 weeks after treatment
The rash looks infected
You are pregnant or treating a baby under 2 months

name: Impetigo
overview: Impetigo is a common and contagious skin infection that causes sores and blisters. It is most common in young children. It is not usually serious and often improves within a week of treatment.
symptoms: Red sores or blisters that burst and leave crusty, golden-brown patches
Often around the nose and mouth, but can be anywhere
Itching
Sores that spread
causes: Bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus infecting the skin
Often through broken skin from cuts, insect bites or eczema
riskFactors: Close contact settings such as nurseries and schools
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses impetigo by looking at the sores; a swab may be taken if it keeps coming back.
treatment: Antiseptic or antibiotic cream prescribed by a doctor or recommended by a pharmacist
Antibiotic tablets if widespread or severe
selfCare: Wash sores gently with warm soapy water
Do not share towels or flannels
Stay off school or work until sores have crusted and healed, or 48 hours after starting antibiotics
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you or your child has impetigo
Symptoms do not improve within 7 days of treatment
Impetigo keeps coming back
emergencySigns: Sores spreading rapidly with high temperature and feeling very unwell

name: Osteoarthritis
overview: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis, causing joints to become painful and stiff. It most often affects the knees, hips and small joints of the hands. Exercise, weight management and pain relief help most people stay active.
symptoms: Joint pain and stiffness, often worse after rest or at the end of the day
Joint swelling
Reduced range of movement
A grating or crackling feeling in the joint
Weakness and loss of muscle around the joint
causes: Gradual damage to the cartilage lining the joint, with the body's repair process changing the joint
Previous joint injury or surgery
Other joint conditions such as gout or rheumatoid arthritis
riskFactors: Jobs involving repetitive stress on joints
diagnosis: A GP usually diagnoses osteoarthritis from symptoms and an examination; X-rays or blood tests are sometimes used to rule out other conditions.
treatment: Exercise and physiotherapy to strengthen muscles
Weight loss if overweight
Painkillers and anti-inflammatory creams or tablets
Steroid injections, or joint replacement surgery for severe cases
selfCare: Stay active with low-impact exercise such as walking, swimming or cycling
Use heat or cold packs for pain
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent joint pain or stiffness
Joint pain affecting daily activities
Pain not controlled by simple painkillers
emergencySigns: A hot, red, swollen joint with fever (possible joint infection)
Sudden inability to bear weight after a fall

name: Rheumatoid arthritis
overview: Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term condition where the immune system attacks the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness. It usually affects the hands, feet and wrists on both sides of the body. Early treatment helps prevent joint damage.
symptoms: Painful, swollen joints, often the same joints on both sides
Stiffness, especially in the morning, lasting more than 30 minutes
Tiredness and low energy
High temperature, sweating and weight loss in some people
Firm lumps under the skin near joints
causes: The immune system attacking the lining of the joints (an autoimmune condition)
A mix of genetic and environmental factors
diagnosis: RA is diagnosed by a GP and rheumatologist using an examination, blood tests for inflammation and antibodies, and X-rays or scans.
treatment: Disease-modifying medicines to slow the disease
Biological and targeted medicines
Painkillers and short-term steroids for flare-ups
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and sometimes surgery
selfCare: Stay active with regular gentle exercise
whenToSeeDoctor: Joint pain, swelling or stiffness lasting more than a few weeks
Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
Flare-ups or side effects if you already have RA
emergencySigns: A single hot, swollen, painful joint with high temperature (possible joint infection)
Fever or signs of serious infection while on immune-suppressing medicine

name: Gout
overview: Gout is a type of arthritis where crystals form inside joints, causing sudden attacks of severe pain and swelling. It often affects the big toe. Attacks can be treated, and long-term medicines and lifestyle changes help prevent them.
symptoms: Sudden severe pain in a joint, often the big toe
Hot, swollen, red skin over the joint (may be less visible on darker skin)
Extreme tenderness, even to light touch
Attacks often start at night
causes: Too much uric acid in the blood, which forms crystals in the joints
Triggers include alcohol, sugary drinks, some foods such as red meat and seafood, and some medicines
riskFactors: High blood pressure, diabetes or kidney disease
Drinking alcohol, especially beer and spirits
diagnosis: Gout is diagnosed from symptoms and a blood test for uric acid; sometimes fluid is taken from the joint to look for crystals.
treatment: Anti-inflammatory medicines or steroids to treat attacks
Long-term medicines to lower uric acid, prescribed by a doctor
Lifestyle changes
selfCare: Rest and raise the joint during an attack
Use an ice pack wrapped in a towel
Cut down on alcohol and sugary drinks
prevention: Take uric acid-lowering medicine as prescribed
whenToSeeDoctor: Sudden severe joint pain
Repeated attacks
Attacks not improving with treatment
emergencySigns: A hot, painful joint with high temperature and feeling unwell (possible joint infection)

name: Osteoporosis
overview: Osteoporosis is a condition that weakens bones, making them fragile and more likely to break. It develops slowly over years and is often only found after a fall or minor injury causes a fracture. Treatment and lifestyle changes help strengthen bones.
symptoms: Usually no symptoms until a bone breaks
Broken bones after a minor fall, often in the wrist, hip or spine
Loss of height or a stooped posture
Sudden back pain from a spinal fracture
causes: Natural bone loss with age
Hormonal changes, especially falling oestrogen after menopause
Some medicines such as long-term steroids
Medical conditions affecting hormones or nutrient absorption
riskFactors: Family history of osteoporosis or hip fracture
diagnosis: Osteoporosis is diagnosed with a bone density scan (DEXA), often alongside a fracture risk assessment.
treatment: Medicines to strengthen bones, prescribed by a doctor
Calcium and vitamin D supplements if needed
Hormone therapy for some people
Falls prevention
selfCare: Eat a diet rich in calcium
prevention: Calcium-rich diet and enough vitamin D
whenToSeeDoctor: You have risk factors and are worried
A bone breaks after a minor fall
Loss of height or curving of the spine
emergencySigns: Unable to stand or bear weight after a fall, or severe pain in the hip or back
A visibly deformed limb after a fall

name: Back pain
overview: Back pain, especially in the lower back, is very common. It usually gets better within a few weeks or months. Staying active is one of the most helpful things you can do.
symptoms: Aching or stiffness anywhere along the spine
Sharp, localised pain
Pain that may spread to the buttocks or legs
Pain that is worse when bending, lifting or sitting for long periods
causes: Often no specific cause (non-specific back pain)
Strains or sprains from lifting or twisting
Poor posture or long periods of sitting
Conditions such as a slipped disc, sciatica or osteoarthritis
diagnosis: A GP or physiotherapist diagnoses back pain through questions and an examination; scans are usually not needed unless there are warning signs.
treatment: Staying active and continuing normal activities
Painkillers such as anti-inflammatory medicines
Exercises and physiotherapy
Talking therapies for long-term pain
selfCare: Do gentle back exercises and stretches
prevention: Regular exercise such as walking, swimming or yoga
whenToSeeDoctor: Pain does not improve after a few weeks
Pain stops you doing daily activities
Pain is very bad or getting worse
You also have numbness, tingling or weakness
emergencySigns: Numbness around the genitals or bottom
Loss of bladder or bowel control, or unable to pee
Weakness or numbness in both legs
Back pain with high temperature, or after a serious fall or accident
Severe pain with chest pain

name: Sciatica
overview: Sciatica is pain caused by irritation or compression of the sciatic nerve, which runs from the lower back down the legs. It usually gets better within 4 to 6 weeks, but can last longer.
symptoms: Pain, tingling or numbness in the bottom, back of the leg, foot and toes
Pain usually on one side
Pain that is worse when moving, sneezing or coughing
Weakness in the leg
causes: A slipped (herniated) disc pressing on the nerve
Narrowing of the spinal canal (spinal stenosis)
Injury to the spine
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses sciatica from symptoms and an examination; scans are only needed in some cases.
treatment: Staying active and doing exercises
Painkillers
Physiotherapy
Steroid injections or surgery in some cases
selfCare: Keep moving and continue normal activities as much as possible
whenToSeeDoctor: Pain has not improved after a few weeks
Pain is getting worse or stopping daily activities
Pain in both legs
emergencySigns: Numbness around the genitals or bottom
Loss of bladder or bowel control or unable to pee
Weakness or numbness in both legs that is getting worse

name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
overview: Carpal tunnel syndrome is pressure on a nerve in the wrist that causes tingling, numbness and pain in the hand and fingers. It is common and often gets better with simple treatments.
symptoms: Tingling or pins and needles in the thumb, index and middle fingers
Numbness or pain in the hand and fingers
Symptoms often worse at night
Weak thumb or difficulty gripping
causes: Pressure on the median nerve as it passes through a narrow channel in the wrist (the carpal tunnel)
Swelling in the wrist, for example from repetitive use, pregnancy, injury or arthritis
riskFactors: Diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis or an underactive thyroid
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses carpal tunnel syndrome from symptoms and an examination; nerve conduction tests may be used.
treatment: Wrist splints, especially at night
Painkillers
Steroid injections
Surgery to release pressure on the nerve if symptoms persist
selfCare: Wear a wrist splint at night
prevention: Take regular breaks from repetitive hand movements
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms not improving after a few weeks
Symptoms affecting sleep or daily activities
Constant numbness or weakness in the hand
emergencySigns: Sudden numbness or weakness in one arm or hand with face drooping or speech problems (possible stroke)
